content: The systematic reviews were conducted to evaluate the evidence for the PICO (Population, Intervention, Comparator, Outcome) questions and their outcomes using a standardized methodology. Titles, abstracts, and full texts of potentially relevant literature were screened with the use of key subject words and text words. Authors and field experts were contacted to identify any missing studies or ongoing research. For the updated ATS/CDC/IDSA TB treatment guidelines, the same groups of reviewers who conducted the systematic reviews also prepared GRADE evidence profiles. These profiles were presented to the Guideline Development Group (GDG) for assessment before and during the GDG meeting. The GRADEpro platform was used to assess evidence quality, including factors such as directness and precision. The strength of recommendations was considered from different perspectives. For patients, a strong recommendation implies that most individuals in a given situation would prefer the recommended course of action, with minimal need for formal decision aids. A conditional recommendation indicates that while many would follow the suggested course, a significant proportion might not. For clinicians, strong recommendations suggest that most patients should receive the intervention, and adherence to these recommendations could serve as a quality or performance indicator. Conditional recommendations require clinicians to help patients make decisions aligned with their values and preferences, potentially using decision aids. For policymakers, strong recommendations can be adopted as policy in most situations, while conditional recommendations may require extensive debate and stakeholder involvement. Relative effects, such as relative risks or odds ratios, were calculated from pooled data in individual or aggregated formats from included studies. Absolute effects and risk differences were used to express the magnitude of effects between intervention and comparator groups. Adjustments were made where possible to reduce bias and confounding. Detailed notes on the GRADE evidence profiles summarizing the systematic review results were provided in an online annex. The GDG meeting, held at WHO headquarters in Geneva in July 2016, involved discussions on evidence for each PICO question. GDG members assessed the evidence and formulated recommendations based on the balance of benefits and harms, patient values and preferences, resource implications, equity, human rights, acceptability, and feasibility. In cases where evidence was insufficient, such as for the use of the Category II regimen for previously treated TB, a good practice statement approach was used instead of a formal recommendation. All decisions were reached through discussion and consensus, without the need for voting. Additional analyses were conducted after the GDG meeting to address gaps in information, leading to slight revisions of two recommendations on treatment supervision options. These revised recommendations were shared with GDG members for review and endorsement. External peer review was conducted by an External Review Group comprising experts and end-users from national programs, technical agencies, and WHO regional offices. The updated guidelines were published on the WHO Global TB Programme website and made freely available in multiple formats and six languages. They were also disseminated through technical meetings, training activities, and peer-reviewed journals. WHO worked with regional and country offices, technical partners, and funding agencies to support the adoption of new recommendations into national TB policies and guidelines. Implementation of the recommendations will be evaluated several years after publication, and the guidelines will be reviewed and updated every 4–5 years or earlier if new evidence emerges. Regarding the effectiveness of 4-month fluoroquinolone-containing regimens compared to the standard 6-month regimen (2HRZE/4HR) for drug-susceptible pulmonary TB, the GDG strongly recommended against the use of shorter fluoroquinolone-containing regimens. Evidence showed significantly higher relapse rates at 18 months follow-up with the 4-month regimens, despite slightly higher culture conversion rates at 2 months. There was no reduction in adverse events or mortality with the shorter regimens. Concerns were raised about the potential for increased fluoroquinolone resistance, which could compromise its use in drug-resistant TB treatment. The GDG supported the continued use of the standard 6-month rifampicin-based regimen. For the use of fixed-dose combination (FDC) tablets compared to separate drug formulations in treating drug-susceptible TB, the GDG conditionally recommended FDCs. Evidence from systematic reviews indicated that FDCs were non-inferior to separate formulations in terms of treatment failure, death, adherence, and adverse events. Patient satisfaction was higher with FDCs, and they offered programmatic benefits such as simplified supply chain management and reduced pill burden. However, concerns about drug bioavailability in FDCs highlighted the need for further research and procurement of FDCs with demonstrated bioavailability. National TB programs were advised to maintain a supply of separate drug formulations for specific treatment conditions and adverse reaction management.
